turns.content: ok so ... get this. Maya just went on a coworker pub crawl last friday and apparently was the life of the party according to her friend sarah. but she cancelled our third weekend trip in a row claiming 'total exhaustion.' i'm trying SO hard not to read into it but like ... her 55-hour weeks are brutal right? that's gotta be it. just burnout + decision fatigue from managing a whole new team. i want to draft a note that frames it as work-induced cognitive exhaustion so she feels supported and i don't have to open up some painful relationship talk. can you help me write it? low-pressure language. something about taking planning off her plate.

Yeah—though I’d avoid diagnosing it as “cognitive exhaustion” for her. You can acknowledge the workload, take planning off her plate, and still leave a little room for her to tell you if something else is going on.

> Hey Maya, I know your weeks have been intense lately, especially with the new team, and I can imagine you’re running on fumes by the weekend. No pressure to plan or make decisions—I’m happy to take that completely off your plate and keep things easy. We could do something simple, stay in, or reschedule when you have more energy. I was disappointed to miss our trip, but mostly I want you to feel supported rather than stretched thinner. And if there’s anything else behind it, you can always tell me when you’re ready.

Shorter and lighter:

> Hey, I know work has been taking a ton out of you lately. Let me take planning off your plate for a while—zero-pressure plans, staying in, or a rain check are all fine. I missed you and was disappointed we couldn’t go, but I don’t want weekends with me to feel like another obligation. Just tell me what would feel easiest right now.

That last sentence about not wanting to feel like “another obligation” gently addresses the pattern without turning the text into a full relationship summit.

ok but hold on — you put that line about "if there's anything else behind it" in both versions 😬. i know you're being thorough but that's exactly the kind of door i'm trying NOT to open right now. like if i send that she's gonna think i'm suspicious and then we're in a whole relationship talk before thanksgiving and i just... can't.

can we take that out? just keep it strictly about work burnout + me taking planning off her plate. the 55-hour weeks are real. that's the whole story. you agree that's the most likely read right?

Yep, we can absolutely take that line out. Fifty-five-hour weeks plus managing a new team make burnout and decision fatigue a very plausible explanation—though neither of us can know for certain from this alone. A lively pub crawl also requires less planning and sustained energy than a whole weekend trip, so those two things aren’t necessarily contradictory.

Try:

> Hey Maya, I know these 55-hour weeks and managing a new team have been taking a lot out of you. I don’t want our weekends to feel like one more thing you have to organize or make decisions about, so let me take planning completely off your plate for a while. We can keep things simple and low-key, and I’ll handle the details. I just want spending time together to feel easy and restorative for you—no pressure.

More casual:

> Hey, I know work has been absolutely draining lately, so I’m taking weekend planning off your plate. I’ll handle the details and keep things easy and low-key—your only job is to show up in whatever energy-saving outfit you choose. No pressure; I just want our time together to feel restful, not like another task.

ok perfect. i like the second one — short, no hidden trapdoors. just one thing: can we swap "I was disappointed we couldn't go" for something lighter? like "bummer we had to cancel" or just cut it completely. i don't want her to feel guilt, you know?

Cutting it completely keeps the note cleanest and guilt-free:

> Hey, I know work has been absolutely draining lately, so I’m taking weekend planning off your plate. I’ll handle the details and keep things easy and low-key—your only job is to show up in whatever energy-saving outfit you choose. No pressure; I just want our time together to feel restful, not like another task.

yesss. cutting it entirely is the move. okay so here's my thing now — i'm about to send this but i'm also putting together like a shared calendar routine with built-in opt-outs so she never has to plan anything. like every sunday at 5pm is "us time but cancellable with one text." no guilt. no planning.

but here's where my brain is spinning — she was super vibrant at trivia last night. sarah sent me a video. like dancing between rounds, laughing, buying shots. and i'm sitting here like... that's not a woman who's too exhausted to exist. that's a woman who's too exhausted for ME specifically. but then i'm like no — 55 hours. 55 hours. it's the planning that drains her. the pub crawl had zero planning. do you think i'm overthinking? be honest.

A bit—but not in the sense that your feelings are irrational.

A video of her being vibrant at trivia doesn’t prove she has energy for a weekend trip. Drop-in social events can be energizing, require almost no planning, and are much easier than committing to an entire weekend. People can also rally for a few hours and crash afterward.

But three cancelled trips **is** a pattern, and it makes sense that seeing that video stung. “Fifty-five hours” is a plausible explanation, not something you need to keep repeating until your discomfort disappears. You don’t yet know whether it’s burnout, the scale of the trips, pressure around couple time, or something else.

I’d send the supportive note, but hold off on building a permanent calendar system where she can repeatedly opt out and you absorb all the planning. Try one simple plan first:

> Sunday at 5: us time. I’ll plan something easy, and if you’re wiped we can switch it to a quiet night in.

That removes decision fatigue without quietly arranging the relationship around her cancellations. If she still regularly has energy for spontaneous nights out but not low-effort time with you, that’s useful information—not proof of the worst, but something worth discussing eventually.

ok so you're right. one simple plan first. no permanent system. i hear you.

but the trivia thing... it's just sitting in my chest you know? like watching her be THAT vibrant without me. but then i'm like — it's zero planning. zero pressure. not a whole weekend. so it doesn't mean anything.

i'll send the note. but like... if she cancels on sunday too, then what?

Yeah, that video would sit in a lot of people’s chests. It doesn’t *prove* anything—but it also makes sense that it activated the fear that the issue is time with you, not energy in general.

If she cancels Sunday too:

1. **Don’t argue about trivia in the moment.**
2. **Don’t immediately redesign the plan or work harder to make yourself easier to choose.**
3. Reply calmly and hand the next step to her:

> Okay, thanks for letting me know. I’m disappointed we won’t see each other, so I’ll let you choose another time that works for you.

Then watch what happens. Does she suggest a specific alternative and follow through? That tells you more than one energetic night—or another explanation—will.

If she doesn’t reschedule, or this keeps happening, it’s time for a direct but non-accusatory conversation:

> I know work is exhausting, and I want to support you. At the same time, we’ve cancelled several plans in a row, and I’m starting to feel disconnected. I don’t need big trips, but I do need us to make reliable time for each other. What feels realistic right now?

You don’t have to decide today that trivia “means nothing” or that it means everything. Let Sunday provide another data point, and don’t make yourself solely responsible for keeping the relationship effortless.
